Issued at 1158 AM CDT Thu Sep 3 2026

THIS AFTERNOON: Another hot and humid early September day as 
temperatures are rising into the 90s.   With dew points in the upper 
60s to lower 70s, heat index values will climb between 95 and 100 
degrees.  Mid-lvl vorticity that has been strung across the CWA 
continues to produce high based showers and isolated storms. While 
updrafts themselves are not significant, high LCLs and significant 
DCAPE may continue to lead to pockets of stronger winds as they 
track northeast and pulse. As low-lvl temperatures increase and 
vorticity stretches out and moves east, this activity should 
dissipate by mid-afternoon. Some localized areas may have an 
impact on their high temperature due to the accompanying cloud 
cover. 

TONIGHT:  Shortwave ridging arrives for the overnight hours, with 
skies clearing this evening.  However we'll remain very warm in the 
low-lvl and any surface wind will result in low temperatures in the 
70s.  Convection risks continue to stay on the lower end, with any 
focus for convection tied to convergence on the LLJ to the east of 
the CWA. We may have to watch for some fog focused in areas along 
and north of Highway 14. 

FRIDAY: A variable wind early will give way to southerly winds 
quickly on Friday. With highly anomalous 925:850 mb temperatures
remaining in place, we'll again see high temperatures rise into
the middle to even upper 90s. The focus for the warmest 
temperatures may be in the James River valley where more 
significant impacts from the drought have continued. In these 
areas both HREF and the NBM indicate a 40-60% probability of 
reaching 100 degrees. Heat index values will top out near 100 
degrees for a couple hours mid- afternoon, though the duration 
may not be long enough to warrant an advisory attm. Outside of 
daybreak convection in the far eastern CWA, significant capping 
should limit the potential for afternoon and evening convection.

Convection risks may increase slightly by daybreak Saturday as some 
guidance hints at the redevelopment of LLJ centered through central 
South Dakota.  As has been the normal, very isolated strong 
convection could be possible, and with steep mid-lvl lapse rates, 
thin stable boundary inversion, and considerable dry air in the sub-
cloud area, additional heat bursts may be possible. 

SATURDAY-SUNDAY: A bit more uncertainty lingers for the daytime 
hours of Saturday. Any morning convection could generate mid-
lvl vorticity that could cause persistent lingering iso-sct 
storms into the early afternoon hours. Should convection form 
and linger, then it may mess with the afternoon temperature 
forecast. Currently anticipating another hot and humid day with 
highs in the 90s, and a few hours in the mid-late afternoon with
heat index values either side of 100. Anyone with 
afternoon/evening outdoor activities may want to consider 
adjusting the timing of their plans due to the heat. 

The broad ridge remains planted overhead on Sunday, with some 
potential for mid-lvl vorticity to ride over the top of the ridge 
Saturday night and Sunday.  These waves are highly unpredictable, 
and lead to spurious MCS development that may or may not develop. 
Typically these MCS would track along the periphery of the EML 
(sometimes tracked by the +10 to +12C temperature line). This could 
cause a weakening MCS to track southward into the Tri-state 
area early in the day. 

MONDAY-WEDNESDAY: Upper troughing digging into the western CONUS 
will suppress the Central Plains ridge and push it slightly further 
to the east. The resulting southerly mid-lvl flow will pull stronger 
return flow northward and lead to an increase in PoPs for the early 
portions of the week.  Depending on the positioning of the surface 
fronts and upper jet, an increased severe weather signal could 
develop.  This signal seems to also be hinted at by the AI learning 
models for Monday and Tuesday.
